newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish leasing companies aim to diversify.
newsitem.headline: Turkish leasing companies aim to diversify.

text.p: Turkish leasing companies are aiming to enter into new sectors to achieve a turnover target of $1.6 billion in 1997 after $1.5 billion last year, an official from a leading leasing company said.
"We are aiming at least $1.6 billion in turnover this year," said Erdogan Kahyaoglu, assistant manager of Garanti Leasing.

"We want to raise the share of the leasing sector in the total fixed value investments to 20 percent, as in Europe and the United States, from seven to eight percent now," he told Reuters on the sidelines of an international leasing meeting in Istanbul.
Starting with foodstuffs, Turkey's leasing companies were preparing to enter into new sectors, including the energy and infrastructure markets, he said.
"Energy and infrastructure sectors usually need resources in big amounts and therefore have not used leasing funds," he said.
"But now it is possible to set up international partnerships (in leasing) which enable such sectors to benefit from leasing," he said.
Turkey's leasing sector, launched in late 1980's after a national move towards free market economy, has hit several legal hitches that capped its growth, he said.
Legislative uncertainty in automobile and real estate leasing and high costs were a big obstacle hampering the growth of leasing in Turkey, he said.
But the market share of leased machine equipment was roughly the same as in Europe, Kahyaoglu said.
The leasing sector saw a turnover of $1.2 billion in 1993, which dropped to $500 million in 1994 following a severe economic crisis in Turkey, but bounced back to $1 billion in 1995, he said.
He said small-sized industries and workshops, know as KOBI in Turkey, have shown significant interest in leasing to finance their equipment and other needs.

KOBI companies are usually financed by the state-run Halkbank for their investments but the bank's slow red tape and stringent credit limits scare off KOBI owners to others sources of financing such as leasing, he said.
"Halkbank gives low-interest credits but its standard applications freightens off small investors," he said.
"The leasing sector offers KOBI firms benefits like funds exempt from value added tax," he said.

He said the sector in Turkey had reached the point of operational leasing, which offers short-term finances for investors, but Turkey's leasing law, which bans leasing periods shorter than four years, should be changed.
